subject: partially missing data in bivariate normal distribution

messages.author: f6e5e26ed77eaab6
messages.subject: partially missing data in bivariate normal distribution
parts:
Dear Stan users:

I am new to using Rstan and I would like to implement a previous working model coded in R2WinBUGS to Rstan.

My data is bivariate and normally distributed. yi=(yi1,yi2) for i=1...n and I would like to fit a multivariate normal model. However there are some missing data on yi2 for some observations but their yi1 are all present. I read chapter 8 and searched for relevant topics within the group but I do not seem to find a solution to import my data set into Rstan as my some of my observations are partially missing. Are there any examples or documents that I could read up to solve my very trivial problem?

Thanks in advance,
Jaslene

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] partially missing data in bivariate normal distribution
parts:
You're providing the first column of cr_miss, so you should make the data you pass in a vector.

In parameters, you're estimating the second column of cr_miss, so that should be a parameter vector.

In transformed parameters, you'll want to declare cr_miss as a matrix with the first column being data and the second being parameters.


There might be a more clever way to do it, but it's late and I'm not so familiar with what you're trying to do. (I didn't actually try to read your Stan program.)


Daniel

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] partially missing data in bivariate normal distribution
parts:
Jaslene,

If everything is bivariate Gaussian then you can do everything analytically.

First, split your data into non-missing (which will be two-dimensional)
and missing the second component (which will be one-dimensional).

The non-missing data will be distributed according to the bivariate
Gaussian that you quoted

(y_1, y_2) ~ multi_normal( (mu_1, mu_2), Sigma ),

where Sigma is the 2x2 covariance matrix.

In order to construct the distribution of the missing data we have to
marginalize y_{2} out of the bivariate Gaussian.  Fortunately, this
is straightforward,

y_1 ~ normal(mu_1, sigma_1),

where sigma_1 is the square root of Sigma_{11}.

Your Stan model would then look _something_ like

data {
  int N_nonmiss;
  vector[2] y_nonmiss[N_nonmiss];
  int N_miss;
  real y_miss[N_miss];
}

parameters {
  vector[2] mu;
  cov_matrix[2] Sigma;
}

model {
  // Prior on mu
  // Prior on Sigma, see the manual for examples

  y_nonmiss ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma);
  y_miss ~ normal(mu[1], sqrt(Sigma[1, 1]);

}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] partially missing data in bivariate normal distribution
parts:
Cool. I'm going to add that example to the manual:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1238#issuecomment-224378060

I'd rename the variable Michael called y_miss because
it's actually the observed y[n,1], not the missing
y[n,2].

The only drawback is that it doesn't impute the missing
data for you. If you need to do that, there's probably
a way to analytically derive the conditional

p(y[n,2] | y[n,1], mu, Sigma)

Then you could add that to the generated quantities block
for maximum efficiency (both in per iteration time and
N_eff per iteration). Or declare the y[n,2] as parameters if
you need to use them elsewhere.

- Bob

> https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1238#issuecomment-224378060
>
> I'd rename the variable Michael called y_miss because
> it's actually the observed y[n,1], not the missing
> y[n,2].
>
> The only drawback is that it doesn't impute the missing
> data for you. If you need to do that, there's probably
> a way to analytically derive the conditional
>
> p(y[n,2] | y[n,1], mu, Sigma)
>
> Then you could add that to the generated quantities block
> for maximum efficiency (both in per iteration time and
> N_eff per iteration). Or declare the y[n,2] as parameters if
> you need to use them elsewhere.
>
> - Bob

parts:
Indeed.

The default BUGS/JAGS approach is probably not the model of
missingness most people are after. I had a nice discussion of
this with Merlise Clyde of Duke in the last plus one MCMCski --- she
was telling me about the lengths she went to coding up models for missing data
in BUGS/JAGS (but I don't have a reference) conditioned on other data.
When you do that and define a proper joint distribution, the code
looks much more like Stan code than the direct approach of just plugging
NA into a full-data model.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] partially missing data in bivariate normal distribution
parts:
That's just a warning that there was a numerical issue that
was trapped. As the message says, if there aren't very many
of these, you don't have to worry abot it.

To get rid of them, you can try increasing adapt_delta with

control=list(adapt_delta = 0.99)

and see if that helps. These issues arise when numerical
stability problems creep in under the hood with the Hamiltonian
simulation coupled to the unconstraining transforms plus Jacobians
that we apply automatically.

- Bob
